facts.text: The Treasury argued that the applicant did not have the capacity to acquire immovable property and that the property was not mentioned in its 1936 declaration, so it was not entitled to the title.

facts.text: On 19 December 1994 an expert report concluded that the applicant foundation’s title should be annulled as it lacked capacity to acquire immovable property and the property should be re-registered in the name of former owners.

issues.text: Whether the legislation on foundations and its interpretation by domestic courts interfered with the applicant's right to the peaceful enjoyment of its possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1

anchor.surface_text: The applicant alleged, in particular, that the legislation on foundations and the interpretation thereof by the domestic courts, had interfered with its right to the peaceful enjoyment of its possessions, as guaranteed by Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

issues.text: Whether the applicant foundation had a "possession" within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1

anchor.surface_text: The Government argued that the applicant foundation did not have a “possession” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. That provision only applied to property actually owned and the annulment of the applicant’s title corresponded simply to the rectification of a registration error.

issues.text: Whether the interference with the applicant's property rights complied with the requirement of lawfulness under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1

anchor.surface_text: The first and most important requirement of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 is that any interference by a public authority with the peaceful enjoyment of possessions should be lawful. The rule of law, one of the fundamental principles of a democratic society, is inherent in all the Articles of the Convention

issues.text: Whether the judicial interpretation in 1974 restricting foundations' capacity to acquire immovable property was foreseeable and accessible to the applicant foundation at the time of its acquisitions in 1952 and 1958

anchor.surface_text: Consequently, the annulment of the title to the property in question, pursuant to case-law adopted sixteen and twenty-two years respectively after its acquisition, was not foreseeable for the applicant foundation. It could not reasonably have foreseen that its title, obtained many years earlier, would one day be annulled because of a new judicial interpretation of the applicable legislation

issues.text: Whether the applicant foundation's title to the property was lawfully acquired and protected under domestic law at the time of acquisition

anchor.surface_text: The Court finds that it is not in doubt that, at the time of the acquisitions in 1952 and 1958, the applicant foundation was certain of having acquired the property lawfully under the then applicable Turkish law. Moreover, until the 1974 case-law was adopted, it had the “legal certainty” that it was entitled to acquire immovable property.

issues.text: Whether the restriction on the applicant foundation's capacity to acquire immovable property was based on a proper legal basis and consistent with the margin of appreciation afforded to Contracting States

anchor.surface_text: Contracting States should enjoy a wide margin of appreciation in regulating the acquisition of land and other immovable property by legal entities such as foundations. anchor.surface_text: The case originated in an application (no. 34478/97) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a foundation existing under the laws of Turkey, Fener Rum Erkek Lisesi Vakfı (“the applicant”), on 25 November 1996.

arguments.claim: There had been no legal basis on which to prohibit the applicant foundation from acquiring immovable property, resulting in annulment of its title.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant foundation mainly argued that there had been no legal basis on which to prohibit it from acquiring immovable property, as a result of which its title to property had been annulled.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that the interference did not comply with the requirement of lawfulness as the restriction was based on a judicial interpretation adopted after the acquisitions, not on clear legislation.

arguments.claim: The prohibition on acquiring immovable property was not provided by legislation but based on 1974 Court of Cassation case-law treating 1936 declarations as constitutive instruments limiting acquisition capacity.

anchor.surface_text: It observed that the prohibition in question was not provided for by legislation but was based on the case-law of the Court of Cassation. That court, in a judgment of 8 May 1974, had decided that the declarations made in 1936 by religious minorities’ foundations were to be regarded as the constitutive instruments of the vakıf (foundations), finalising their constitutions.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court noted that the restriction arose from the 1974 judicial interpretation, not from the legislation in force at the time of acquisition.

arguments.claim: The applicant foundation did not have a "possession" within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; annulment of title was a rectification of a registration error.

anchor.surface_text: The Government argued that the applicant foundation did not have a possession within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. That provision only applied to property actually owned and the annulment of the applicants title corresponded simply to the rectification of a registration error.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the applicant had acquired the property lawfully and had legal certainty until 1974, thus it had possession under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

arguments.claim: Even if interference occurred, it concerned a restriction on capacity to acquire immovable property based on foundation constitutions and legislation.

anchor.surface_text: In the alternative, the Government contended that, even supposing that there had been interference with the applicants right under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the matter simply concerned a restriction imposed on the capacity to acquire immovable property.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court acknowledged States have a wide margin of appreciation to regulate acquisition capacity but found the interference was not lawful due to lack of foreseeability and clarity.

arguments.claim: Foundations are entitled to acquire immovable property only as provided in their constitutions; the applicant foundation lacked such capacity as it was not reserved in its 1936 declaration.

anchor.surface_text: The Government pointed out that foundations were entitled to acquire immovable property only to the extent provided for in their constitutions. If the applicant foundation was not so entitled, this had to be regarded as the consequence of the fact that, in its declaration of 1936, it had not reserved for itself the legal capacity to acquire other immovable property by purchase or donation.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no legislative provision prohibited acquisition beyond the 1936 declaration and that the applicant had legal certainty at the time of acquisition.

arguments.claim: The 1936 declaration was the foundation's constitutive instrument covering all immovable property; absence of express provision precluded acquisition of other property.

anchor.surface_text: The Government further submitted that the applicant foundation had acquired legal personality after filing the declaration in question in March 1936. That declaration was the foundations constitutive instrument, covering all the immovable property in its possession. The foundation thus recognised had also been required to include therein an express provision for the acquisition of other property by purchase or donation, failing which it was precluded from relying on such legal capacity to acquire other immovable property.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the legislation silent on this and that the judicial interpretation was not foreseeable at the time of acquisition.

arguments.claim: The acquisition of immovable property by the applicant foundation was outside its legal capacities and domestic courts annulled it to protect public interest.

anchor.surface_text: Consequently, the acquisition of immovable property by the applicant foundation was an act that had not fallen within its legal capacities and it was the task of the domestic courts to protect the public interest by annulling an acquisition that was devoid of legal basis.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the annulment was not based on a clear legal basis and was unforeseeable, breaching the requirement of lawfulness.

arguments.claim: The 1936 declarations by foundations of religious communities are constitutive instruments and cannot be amended for public policy reasons.

anchor.surface_text: In the grounds for its decision, relying on the judgment of the combined civil divisions of the Court of Cassation of 8 May 1974, the Directorate observed that the 1936 declarations by foundations of religious communities were to be regarded as the constitutive instruments of those establishments and that amendment of those constitutions was impossible for reasons of public policy.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that the judicial interpretation was not foreseeable at the time of acquisition and that the applicant had legal certainty until 1974.

arguments.claim: The striking-out of the applicant's title from the land register did not take place until 2002, supported by evidence of fines for unauthorized building works in 2001.

anchor.surface_text: The Government argued that the striking-out of the applicants title from the land register did not take place until 2002. In this connection they referred to a decision taken by the Beyolu Municipal Council on 13 March 2001 whereby the applicant foundation, as owner, together with its tenant, had been fined for adding an additional storey onto the building without authorisation.

arguments.claim: At the time of acquisitions in 1952 and 1958, the applicant foundation was certain of having acquired the property lawfully under Turkish law and had legal certainty of entitlement.

anchor.surface_text: In this connection the Court observes that the acquisition of 10October 1952 was validated by a certificate issued by the Istanbul Governors office on 3 October 1952 (see paragraph 12 above). This document, drawn up on the basis of the Land Registry Act (Law no. 2644 of 22 December 1934), expressly mentioned that the applicant foundation, as a legal entity, was entitled to acquire immovable property. This was also the case for the acquisition by purchase of 16 December 1958.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the applicant had legal certainty and lawful acquisition at the time, supported by official certificates.

arguments.claim: The annulment of the title pursuant to case-law adopted 16 and 22 years after acquisition was not foreseeable and thus breached the requirement of lawfulness under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

anchor.surface_text: Consequently, the annulment of the title to the property in question, pursuant to case-law adopted sixteen and twenty-two years respectively after its acquisition, was not foreseeable for the applicant foundation. It could not reasonably have foreseen that its title, obtained many years earlier, would one day be annulled because of a new judicial interpretation of the applicable legislation

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court emphasized the importance of foreseeability and legal certainty, which were lacking due to the late judicial interpretation.

arguments.claim: Contracting States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation in regulating acquisition of immovable property by legal entities and may implement necessary measures to protect public policy and interests.

anchor.surface_text: Contracting States should enjoy a wide margin of appreciation in regulating the acquisition of land and other immovable property by legal entities such as foundations. They are thus entitled to implement the necessary measures, in accordance with the general interest, in order to ensure that such entities can pursue their declared aims and objectives and to protect public policy and the interests of their members.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court acknowledged the margin of appreciation but found the interference was not lawful due to lack of foreseeability and clarity.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT UNANIMOUSLY

1.  Holds that there has been a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found that the interference with the applicant foundation's property rights was not lawful because the restriction was based on a judicial interpretation adopted after the acquisitions, lacking foreseeability and clarity, breaching Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

holdings.text: Holds that the respondent State is to re-register the disputed immovable property in the land register in the name of the applicant foundation, within three months from the date on which the judgment becomes final

anchor.surface_text:
3.  Holds

(a)  that the respondent State is to re-register the disputed immovable property in the land register in the name of the applicant foundation, within three months from the date on which the judgment becomes final in accordance with Article 44 § 2 of the Convention;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court ordered the respondent State to remedy the violation by re-registering the disputed property in the applicant's name to restore its peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

holdings.text: Holds that if the property is not re-registered, the respondent State is to pay the applicant foundation EUR 890,000 in respect of pecuniary damage

anchor.surface_text: (b)  that if the property is not re-registered, the respondent State is to pay the applicant foundation, within the same three-month time-limit, EUR 890,000 (eight hundred and ninety thousand euros) in respect of pecuniary damage, to be converted into new Turkish liras at the rate applicable at the date of settlement;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court provided an alternative remedy of monetary compensation for pecuniary damage if the property is not re-registered, reflecting the current value of the property and loss from non-enjoyment.
